title: SEPTEMBER IS SUCIDE PREVENTION MONTH
author: NK Udada Foundation
body:
At the start of September, we opened Suicide Prevention Month with a post on the myths and facts around suicide. We wanted to clear up the misunderstandings that keep people silent and stop them reaching out for help.
As the month closes, it feels right to look back at what we covered and ask what happens next. Awareness cannot stop at the end of a campaign. It has to become something we carry into how we treat each other every day.
What we learned
Our myths and facts post challenged some common but harmful ideas:
•	Myth: Asking someone if they are suicidal puts the idea in their head. Fact: Asking directly, calmly and without judgement does not increase risk. It often brings relief.
•	Myth: People who talk about suicide just want attention. Fact: Talking about it is often a genuine warning sign and should always be taken seriously.
•	Myth: Only people with a diagnosed mental illness think about suicide. Fact: Suicidal thoughts can affect anyone, especially during overwhelming stress, loss or crisis.
•	Myth: Once someone has decided, there is nothing anyone can do. Fact: Most people who feel suicidal are ambivalent. Connection and timely support can change the outcome.
We also shared the warning signs to watch for, from withdrawal and hopelessness to sudden calm after a period of low mood, and the risk and protective factors that shape someone's likelihood of reaching crisis point.
Beyond September
A ribbon and a hashtag can only do so much. The real work is in the ordinary moments: noticing when a friend has gone quiet, asking a direct question instead of a polite one, and staying in the room after someone tells you something hard.
At NK UDADA Foundation, we see this as work that continues all year. It shows up in how we support our volunteers, how we run our outreach programs, and how we talk about mental health in the communities we serve. Prevention is not a single month. It is a habit.
Carry it forward
As September ends, we're asking you to keep three things with you:
1.	Check in on someone, even if they seem fine.
2.	Ask directly if you're worried, and listen without rushing to fix.
3.	Know where to point someone towards help, and follow up after that first conversation.
If you or someone you know is struggling, please reach out for support. You do not have to carry it alone, and neither do we. Thank you for walking through this month with us.

By Amina Yarmah
Data Protection Officer
